name: buffet
workload: Google Benchmark microbenchmarks (memcopy, memview, append, split+join) on byte buffers from 8 to 8192 bytes, comparing buffet (a C SSO/refcounted buffer) against std::string/std::string_view and C string functions.
claimed_speedup: SPLITJOIN: buffet 1397 ns vs C++ (std::string) 3317 ns and C 2782 ns, roughly 2.4x faster than std::string (derived from page data). But MEMVIEW: std::string_view 0.609 ns vs buffet 6.36 ns, i.e. buffet is slower there; APPEND results are mixed by size.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++2a -fpermissive -g -O2 (per repo Makefile); benchmark harness is Google Benchmark (src/bench.cpp)
hardware: "weak Core i3" (exact CPU model/generation not stated)
tradeoffs: C API only (no operator overloading); uses reference-counted 'views' that can alias/share a buffer, adding lifetime caveats; GPL-3.0 license restricts embedding in proprietary code; results are workload-dependent (helps bulk split/join, hurts plain memory-view access).
caveats: Author explicitly states "the lib is not much optimized and the bench maybe amateurish"; CPU model is not precisely stated; only libstdc++ (via g++) is exercised, not libc++ or MSVC STL; several sub-benchmarks (MEMVIEW, some APPEND sizes) show std::string/string_view winning, so the 'faster' claim holds only for the split/join workload.
found_via: gh search repos "faster than std::string" (adapted GitHub-search pattern from the blogs/talks source); confirmed via repo README and src/bench.cpp

name: fstring
workload: Unspecified "writing and conversion" operations on a single-header, stack-allocated, fixed-capacity string versus std::string; no operation counts, sizes, or benchmark code are published.
claimed_speedup: "Significantly faster for writing and conversion than std::string (around 2x - 3x faster)" (verbatim from README, no supporting numbers table).
tradeoffs: Requires knowing the maximum string length at compile time (fixed-capacity, not a general-purpose std::string replacement); single header; the '2-3x' figure cannot be independently checked since no benchmark code or data is published.
caveats: No workload description, no compiler/flags, no hardware stated; the claim is unsupported first-party prose in the README with no visible benchmark harness; very low visibility (0 stars, 3 commits).

name: Pool-allocator string (Dicanio STL/ATL/Pool string benchmark)
workload: Building a std::vector of many small wide-character strings via push_back and then sorting it, comparing std::wstring (MSVC STL), ATL CStringW, and strings allocated from a custom fixed-chunk pool allocator.
claimed_speedup: Pool-allocator strings ~42% faster than STL std::wstring and ~47% faster than ATL CStringW for vector creation (sample run: ATL 954 ms, STL 866 ms, Pool 506 ms), per the author's blog post.
hardware: Windows 10 64-bit, Intel i7 (exact model/generation not stated)
tradeoffs: The pool-allocated strings depend on a pre-allocated fixed-size chunk arena rather than being a drop-in std::string replacement, and require managing pool lifetime; the author notes plain STL SSO already wins for tiny strings, so the advantage is specific to bulk creation of many small/medium heap-backed strings.
caveats: First-party single-run benchmark on the author's own blog/repo; CPU model is not exact ("Intel i7" only); only MSVC STL is tested, not libstdc++/libc++; numbers come from "a sample run" with no variance/repeat data; ATL CStringW is a Windows-only baseline included alongside std::wstring, so this is not a pure std::string-only comparison.
found_via: gh search repos "string benchmark" language:C++ -> GiovanniDicanio/StringBenchmarkStlAtlPool README -> linked blog post giodicanio.com/2023/12/01
